title: Book Store CRUD with Drizzle
idea: Each Book Store route becomes one Drizzle query: `select`, `insert`, `update` or `delete`. The controller waits for it with `await`.
points: `select().from(books)` reads rows; `where(eq(books.id, id))` keeps rows whose id equals `id`.
`insert().values()`, `update().set()` and `delete()` write; `.returning()` hands back the row.
`select` and `returning()` give an array: `[book]` takes the first row, or `undefined`.
A failed query rejects; Express 5 sends that error to your error handler.

walk.text: Schema and `db` from the last lessons, inlined so this file runs alone.
`drizzle-kit` is not run here, so raw SQL creates the table and `insert` seeds three books.
`idOf` turns a bad id into 0, which matches no row. `NaN` would make Postgres throw.
Reads: `orderBy` fixes the order, and `[book]` is `undefined` when no row matches.
`insert` plus `returning()` gives back the stored row, with its new `id`.
`update` and `delete` find the row inside the statement. An empty `returning()` means 404.
The routes now point at async controllers; nothing else in Express changes.

code.title: The SQL Drizzle sends
code.caption: `toSQL()` shows the SQL and parameters without sending them. Values travel apart, as `$1` and `$2`.

walk.text: The same schema and `db` as the first snippet.
`toSQL()` returns the SQL text and its parameters. Nothing is sent.
`update` with `where`: two parameters, the new year and the id.
No `where`: the same `update` would change every row. Drizzle allows it.

pitfalls: Forget `await` and the query never runs, and nothing reports an error.
`update` or `delete` without `.where()` changes every row in the table.
`select` without `orderBy` returns rows in no promised order; sort lists by `id`.

options: Error: update needs a where clause
quiz.why: Drizzle lets `update` run without `where`, so it would touch every row. Values travel as `$1`, apart from the SQL text.

takeaway: Await each query; for one-book routes, an empty result means 404.

starters: Why does `update` give back an array instead of one book?
Why use `returning()` instead of a second `select`?
What happens if two requests update the same book at once?
